title: Computer Vision
description: CNNs, image classification, detection, and segmentation — how machines interpret images.
blurb: CNNs, image classification, detection, and segmentation — how machines interpret images.
careerApplications: Computer vision roles (autonomous systems, medical imaging, quality inspection) and general AI/ML roles both expect these fundamentals.

lessons.title: Images as numerical tensors
objectives: Explain how an image is represented as numbers a model can process
Explain how tensor changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect tensor with pixel and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A digital image is a grid of numbers, not a picture in any special sense a computer understands. A grayscale image is a 2D array of pixel intensities (0-255); a color image adds a third dimension for channels (Red, Green, Blue), giving a height x width x 3 tensor.
examples:
import numpy as np
img = np.random.randint(0, 256, size=(224, 224, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
print(img.shape)   # (224, 224, 3) -- height, width, RGB channels
print(img[0,0])     # the RGB values of the top-left pixel, e.g. [120, 45, 200]
commonMistakes: Confusing the order of dimensions (height, width, channels) between frameworks — PyTorch defaults to channels-first (C,H,W), while many image libraries use channels-last (H,W,C); mixing them.
lessons.careerRelevance: This tensor mental model is the entry point to every CV framework and paper you'll ever read.

lessons.title: Image preprocessing
objectives: Apply the standard preprocessing steps before feeding images to a model
Explain how resizing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect resizing with normalization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Raw images vary wildly in size, brightness, and scale — preprocessing standardizes them: resizing to a fixed shape the model expects, normalizing pixel values (often to a 0-1 or standardized range), and sometimes converting color spaces.
examples:
from torchvision import transforms
preprocess = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize((224, 224)),
    transforms.ToTensor(),                 # scales pixel values to [0, 1]
    transforms.Normalize(mean=[0.485,0.456,0.406], std=[0.229,0.224,0.225]),
])
commonMistakes: Normalizing training images but forgetting to apply the EXACT same normalization at inference time — the model then sees inputs on a totally different scale than it was trained on.
lessons.careerRelevance: Preprocessing consistency between training and serving is one of the most common real-world CV production bugs.
lessons.explain: Raw images vary wildly in size, brightness, and scale — preprocessing standardizes them: resizing to a fixed shape the model expects, normalizing pixel values (often to a 0-1 or standardized range), and sometimes converting color spaces.

lessons.title: Convolution fundamentals
objectives: Compute a simple convolution output by hand
Explain how convolution changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect convolution with filter/kernel and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A convolution slides a small filter (e.g. 3x3 numbers) across the image, computing a weighted sum at each position — this is how a CNN detects local patterns like edges.
examples:
# 1D intuition: filter [1, -1] slides across [3, 3, 3, 8, 8, 8]
# position 0: 3*1 + 3*-1 = 0   (no change -- no edge)
# position 2: 3*1 + 8*-1 = -5  (big change -- an edge!)
# this is exactly what a convolution filter detects, just in 2D
commonMistakes: Assuming a convolution 'sees' the whole image at once like a fully-connected layer does — it only looks at a small local window at a time, which is precisely the point (parameter sharing.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to compute a convolution output by hand is a extremely common CV interview screening question.

lessons.title: Filters, feature maps & pooling
objectives: Explain what a feature map represents and why pooling is used
Explain how feature map changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect feature map with max pooling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Applying one filter across the whole image produces a feature map — a 2D grid showing WHERE that pattern appears. A CNN layer typically has many filters, producing many feature maps stacked together.
examples:
# max pooling with a 2x2 window on a feature map:
# [[1, 3], [2, 4]] -> keeps only 4 (the max)
# this shrinks a 224x224 feature map toward something much smaller, layer by layer
commonMistakes: Pooling too aggressively too early — you can throw away spatial detail the network genuinely needed for a fine-grained task like segmentation.
lessons.careerRelevance: Feature maps and pooling are exactly what you're inspecting when visualizing 'what a CNN learned.'

lessons.title: Data augmentation & transfer learning
objectives: Apply augmentation to expand a small dataset, and reuse a pretrained CV model
Explain how data augmentation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data augmentation with transfer learning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data augmentation artificially expands your training data by applying realistic transformations (flips, rotations, crops, color jitter) that don't change the true label, teaching the model to be robust to those variations instead of memorizing exact pixel arrangements.
examples:
transforms.Compose([
    transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(),
    transforms.RandomRotation(15),
    transforms.ColorJitter(brightness=0.2),
])
# same image, label unchanged, but the model now sees more variety

lessons.title: Detection, segmentation & evaluation
objectives: Distinguish classification, detection, and segmentation, and their evaluation metrics
Explain how classification vs detection vs segmentation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect classification vs detection vs segmentation with IoU and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Classification answers 'what is in this image' (one label for the whole image). Object detection answers 'what and WHERE' — drawing bounding boxes around each object, evaluated with IoU (Intersection over Union, how well a predicted box overlaps the true box) and mAP.
examples:
# IoU for a detection box:
# IoU = (area of overlap) / (area of union) between predicted and true box
# IoU > 0.5 is a common 'good enough' threshold for counting a detection as correct
commonMistakes: Using plain classification accuracy to judge a detection or segmentation model — these tasks need their own metrics (IoU/mAP, pixel accuracy/mIoU) since there's no single 'right/wrong' label.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing exactly which of these three tasks a real business problem needs (and why) is a common early scoping question in CV roles.

lessons.title: Bias and dataset quality
objectives: Identify how dataset composition biases a vision model's real-world behavior
Explain how dataset bias changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect dataset bias with representativeness and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A vision model only knows what its training images showed it. A face-detection model trained mostly on one skin tone or lighting condition will perform worse on others; a medical-imaging model trained on one hospital's equipment may not generalize to another's scanners.
examples:
# a real, well-documented failure mode:
# face-detection systems trained predominantly on lighter skin tones
# historically showed measurably higher error rates on darker skin tones
# -- a direct consequence of training data composition, not the algorithm itself
commonMistakes: Assuming a high benchmark accuracy number means the model works equally well for everyone in deployment — aggregate accuracy can hide large performance gaps across subgroups.
lessons.careerRelevance: Bias and dataset quality are now explicit, expected discussion points in CV interviews and are legally significant in some deployed applications (e.g. hiring, law enforcement).

lessons.title: Vision transformers: an introduction
objectives: Connect CNN-based vision to the transformer architecture
Explain how vision transformer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect vision transformer with ViT and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Vision Transformers (ViT) offer an alternative to CNNs for image tasks: instead of convolutional filters sliding over the image, the image is split into patches treated like tokens, then processed with the same self-attention mechanism used for text.
examples:
# CNN: local filters slide across the image, building up feature hierarchies
# ViT: image patches are tokens, self-attention lets any patch attend to any other
# directly, without the same built-in 'locality' assumption CNNs have
commonMistakes: Assuming CNNs are always the right choice for vision tasks -- ViTs are a genuine, increasingly common alternative, especially with large training datasets.
lessons.careerRelevance: Vision transformers are increasingly used in state-of-the-art production computer vision systems, alongside CNNs.

quiz.q: A color image is typically represented as a tensor with shape:
A convolution filter's weights are:
Max pooling primarily achieves:
options: downsampling while keeping the strongest activations

quiz.q: Data augmentation is used to:
options: artificially expand training data with label-preserving transformations

quiz.q: Object detection differs from classification mainly by also predicting:
What does 'height x width x channels' describe?
options: the shape of an image represented as a tensor

quiz.q: What is a channel in an image tensor?
options: one of the color components (like red, green, blue) making up each pixel

quiz.q: Why normalize pixel values before feeding them into a model?
options: it helps training converge more reliably by keeping input values in a consistent, well-scaled range
normalization always changes the image's actual content
models can't process pixel values without normalization existing as a concept, but it has no practical effect

quiz.q: What does a convolution filter/kernel do?
options: slides across the image detecting a specific local pattern, like an edge or texture

quiz.q: What does stride control in a convolution?
options: how far the filter moves between each application, affecting output size

quiz.q: What is a feature map?
options: the output of applying a convolution filter across an image, highlighting where a pattern was detected

quiz.q: What does max pooling do?
options: downsamples a feature map by keeping only the maximum value in each small region
converts the image to a different color format

quiz.q: Why does pooling provide some tolerance to small translations in the image?
options: keeping the max value in a region is less sensitive to the pattern shifting slightly within that region
pooling only affects the color channels

quiz.q: What does a typical CNN architecture combine?
options: convolutional blocks that extract features, followed by a fully-connected head for the final prediction

quiz.q: What is data augmentation?
options: deleting part of the training data
artificially creating modified versions of training images (rotated, flipped, cropped) to increase effective data diversity

quiz.q: Why does data augmentation help a vision model generalize better?
options: it exposes the model to more variation than the original dataset alone contains, reducing overfitting to exact original images
it only affects training speed, not generalization

quiz.q: What distinguishes object detection from image classification?
options: detection identifies AND localizes multiple objects with bounding boxes, while classification assigns one label to the whole image
detection never involves a neural network

quiz.q: What does segmentation do that detection doesn't?
options: assigns a label to every individual pixel, rather than just a bounding box around an object
segmentation only works on grayscale images

quiz.q: What does IoU (Intersection over Union) measure?
options: how much a predicted bounding box overlaps with the true bounding box, used to evaluate detection accuracy
the number of classes in a dataset

quiz.q: What does mAP (mean Average Precision) summarize?
options: detection/classification performance averaged across classes and confidence thresholds
the number of pooling layers used

quiz.q: What is dataset bias, in computer vision?
options: a bug in the training code
when the training data doesn't represent the real-world population or conditions fairly, causing skewed model performance

quiz.q: Why does representativeness in a dataset matter for a vision model's fairness?
options: if certain groups or conditions are underrepresented, the model tends to perform worse specifically for them
all datasets are equally representative by default

quiz.q: Why is label quality important in a vision dataset?
options: label quality has no real effect
incorrect or inconsistent labels directly teach the model wrong associations, capping how good it can ever get
label quality only matters for segmentation tasks

quiz.q: What is a Vision Transformer (ViT)?
options: a type of CNN with extra pooling
a model that applies the transformer's self-attention mechanism to image patches treated as tokens
a loss function specific to images

quiz.q: How does a ViT treat an input image differently from a CNN?
options: it splits the image into patches and treats each patch like a token, rather than sliding convolutional filters across it
ViTs don't process images at all

quiz.q: Why might a ViT need more training data than a CNN to reach comparable performance?
options: CNNs have a built-in assumption of local, spatial structure that ViTs must instead learn from data directly
ViTs are always worse regardless of data
data requirements are identical for both

quiz.q: What does resizing images to a consistent size before training accomplish?
options: most models require fixed-size input, so resizing ensures every image fits the model's expected input shape
resizing always distorts the model's predictions
resizing removes the need for normalization

quiz.q: Why is channel ordering (e.g. RGB vs BGR) something to check when preprocessing images?
options: using the wrong channel order can silently feed a model color information in the wrong arrangement, degrading performance
channel order only affects file size
all libraries use identical channel ordering by default

quiz.q: What does 'feature hierarchy' mean in a CNN?
options: early layers detect simple patterns (edges), while deeper layers combine these into more complex, abstract features
feature hierarchy only applies to text models
hierarchy refers to the order files are loaded in

quiz.q: Why evaluate a vision model on more than just overall accuracy?
options: overall accuracy can hide poor performance on specific classes, groups, or conditions, especially with imbalanced or biased data
accuracy is impossible to compute for vision tasks
